definition_evidence: Local self-government constitutionally recognised (Art. 102) with administrative and financial independence, but scope of competences left to statute and filtered through diffuse constitutional review by the Council of State, Court of Audit, and ordinary courts
notes: Centralised financing and strict fiscal oversight mean constitutional guarantees rarely translate into substantive discretion

definition_evidence: Art. 117 of the Italian Constitution situates municipalities within a regionalised framework; the Corte costituzionale has sometimes protected local discretion in education and social services but frequently upheld regional primacy in health and housing
notes: Municipal space mediated by regional law court doctrine and crisis-era budgetary rules; varies by right (stronger in education than housing/health)

definition_evidence: Art. 140 of the Spanish Constitution provides the clearest textual recognition of municipal autonomy reaffirmed repeatedly by the Constitutional Court, but autonomy remains relational since the Comunidades Autonomas exercise decisive control over housing health and education
notes: Catalonia's devolved framework enables tools such as pre-emption rights in housing and anti-segregation measures in education

definition_evidence: Balanced-budget requirements debt brakes and borrowing-approval procedures curtailed municipal spending autonomy during the financial crisis even in states with entrenched decentralisation
year: ~2008-2015 (Eurozone crisis period; exact years not specified in this passage)
notes: Feeds the proposed 'Crisis Autonomy Loss' indicator (spec Sec.6) -- thesis provides the qualitative mechanism, not a quantified score

definition_evidence: COVID-19 pandemic triggered recentralisation of decision-making in health and social services as emergency legislation reallocated local discretion to national coordination
notes: Same crisis-autonomy dynamic as CONSTR_ALL_01 applied to the pandemic

definition_evidence: Municipal innovation proves transformative only when given a clear legal basis stable finance and workable inter-level coordination so that practices endure beyond pilots election cycles and crises
value_type: thesis core claim (not a scored indicator)
notes: This is the thesis's central theoretical payoff. Directly underpins the proposed 'Institutionalisation Score' (spec Sec.6) -- should be treated as the conceptual anchor for that indicator's validation

definition_evidence: Turin's neighbourhood hubs demonstrate municipal innovation enduring specifically because they are embedded in regional statutes and integrated into national systems
notes: Positive institutionalisation example -- contrast case for COMMIT_ATH_01

definition_evidence: Barcelona combines service delivery with market regulation deploying tools such as pre-emption rights and rent caps
notes: Litigation has curtailed aspects of this housing regulation -- commitment does not equal durability

definition_evidence: Athens has experimented with small-scale projects: renovating derelict municipal buildings, subsidising rents for young adults, and piloting social leasing programmes financed by the Recovery and Resilience Facility
thesis_location: Ch V conclusion / Ch VI, p.233 and 247
notes: Explicitly reliant on external funding and national authorisation -- fragility flagged by the thesis itself

definition_evidence: Athens struggles to convert vacancies into affordable supply; limited stock remains the bottleneck
Turin faces chronic under-provisioning of public housing
Barcelona has grown its regulatory tools to expand stock but still confronts market pressure
Regionalised provision supports coverage in Turin but leaves neighbourhood-level inequities
Barcelona integrates municipal health provision within a broader consortial framework
Athens relies on municipal and solidarity infrastructures to patch coverage gaps
Athens has scaled transitional classes for migrant children but faces geographical clustering

Turin uses neighbourhood schools to integrate newcomers with uneven results; ~40% of families enrol children outside their assigned district, reproducing informal segregation even where formal coverage exists
value_type: quantitative (40% -- the one directly-quantified figure found so far)
thesis_location: Ch III (education), p.98 / referenced Ch VI, p.249
evidence_type: documentary + academic study (Fondazione per la Scuola report)
notes: Direct quantitative data point -- rare in this thesis, most findings are qualitative/documentary

definition_evidence: Barcelona deploys broader anti-segregation programmes backed by regional competences
Barcelona's regulatory instruments on rents and short-term rentals show how municipal authority can soften price pressures
Turin leans more on eviction-prevention and tenant support than on price regulation
Athens depends on national measures and targeted local funds with limited direct leverage over prices
Barcelona's embedding of municipal services eases access for marginalised groups
Turin and Athens continue to struggle with access barriers for migrants and uninsured residents
Turin's community-based outreach and Barcelona's regional support for school choice mitigate exclusion from enrolment procedures
Athens often relies on NGOs to bridge access gaps in enrolment

Athens' reliance on solidarity networks and NGOs shows inclusion 'from below', compensating for thin statutory guarantees but remaining fragile since it depends on voluntary or project-based initiatives
Turin's neighbourhood model knits services together and fosters participation though scaling inclusively requires additional resources
Barcelona mainstreams inclusion through institutional tools: anti-eviction taskforces, migrant schooling support, neighbourhood health programmes

Municipal practice frequently moves in the opposite direction from restrictive national frameworks: schools enrol children regardless of status, clinics attend to the uninsured, housing services intervene to prevent destitution
notes: Core evidence for the Universalism Score proposed in spec Sec.5.5

definition_evidence: Outsourcing services to civil society without clear standards can leave marginalised groups subject to 'postcode lotteries'; durable models formalise universality via ordinances, published data, and multi-year contracting frameworks
notes: Directly relevant to the Administrative Conditionality and Institutionalisation indicators (spec Sec.5.5 and Sec.6)

definition_evidence: Between 2014 and 2021 approximately 34,000 housing units in Athens were listed on Airbnb at least once, initially concentrated in tourist districts (Acropolis, Psyrri) before expanding into residential neighbourhoods (Exarcheia, Kypseli)
thesis_location: Ch V, p.233 (referenced in Ch VI)
notes: Direct quantitative figure -- good candidate for the outcome_variables field in impact.csv

definition_evidence: Spazio Non Solo Mamme provided childcare for young migrant mothers in adult education, serving around 50 mothers per year, before its interruption in 2023 due to vandalism
notes: Illustrates dependence on targeted funding / vulnerability to disruption -- relevant to Policy Durability indicator (spec Sec.6)

definition_evidence: Municipal monitoring data indicate services for children and adolescents with disabilities in Turin currently reach 1538 users
year: n/d (current as of monitoring data cited)

construct: Empirical instance of the Commitment-Impact Matrix
definition_evidence: The thesis explicitly applies its own commitment-impact logic: 'In a Commitment-Impact Matrix, Turin would rank high in commitment but only moderate-to-high in impact' for education, reflecting the tension between ambition and constraint
notes: This is the ONE place the thesis itself applies a commitment/impact rating in matrix terms -- direct textual basis for spec Sec.5.3/5.4/7's proposed indices. Confirms the rating is ordinal/qualitative (high, moderate-to-high), not a numeric score in the source

definition_evidence: Constitutional practice is shaped not only by courts and legislatures but also, indirectly, by municipalities NGOs and grassroots movements (building on Anderson's concept, extended by the author to municipalities as subnational institutions acting 'from below' relative to national constitutions)
evidence_type: thesis argument (building on Anderson; Hirschl and Arban)
notes: Explicitly qualified by the thesis: local practices do not amend constitutions, they shape application/interpretation. Should NOT be operationalised as a numeric score without further methodological work -- flag as concept, not metric

definition_evidence: Decentralisation does not guarantee more democratic or inclusive outcomes -- especially where local elites capture policy levers or exclusionary ordinances persist; localisation can entrench inequality as easily as it can foster innovation
notes: Important normative caveat for the whole project: high 'commitment' or 'capacity' scores must not be read as inherently progressive. Athens evictions and Barcelona empadronamiento access difficulties are given by the thesis as its own counter-examples (Ch VI p.242)

definition_evidence: Italy: Art. 114 recognises municipalities as fundamental entities reinforced by subsidiarity (Art.118) and financial autonomy (Art.119). Spain: Arts. 140-142 guarantee self-government plus limited access to Tribunal Constitucional. Greece: Art.102 recognises municipalities but WITHOUT a general competence clause, confining them to delegated state functions
notes: Direct textual source for the MCC 'legal competence' sub-dimension scoring across all three cities

definition_evidence: Turin and Barcelona exercise authority over urban planning housing and social services though health and education remain largely beyond municipal control; Barcelona leverages its special Charter to push regulatory boundaries especially in housing/anti-discrimination. Athens mainly carries out basic administrative tasks (waste management minor welfare); the Kallikratis reform nominally expanded responsibilities but did not equip municipalities with real policymaking authority
notes: Direct source for the MCC 'regulatory power' sub-dimension

definition_evidence: Turin and Barcelona finance more than half their budgets through local taxes (especially property levies) giving discretion despite dependence on transfers -- but Turin has chronic debt and Spanish fiscal rules prevent Barcelona reinvesting surpluses. Athens: budgets dominated by state transfers, surpluses must go to the Single Treasury Account, borrowing is monitored by the Observatory for Economic Autonomy, and Athens has one of the lowest shares of public expenditure among European municipalities, depending heavily on EU structural funds refugee-related instruments and philanthropy
value_type: quantitative-comparative (>50% local tax financing for Turin/Barcelona vs transfer-dominated Athens)
notes: Direct source for MCC 'fiscal autonomy' sub-dimension. The >50%-local-tax figure is one of the few directly comparable quantitative benchmarks in the whole thesis

definition_evidence: Turin and Barcelona participate in institutionalised (if largely consultative) forums: Italy's Conferenza Stato-Citta and Spain's CNAL. Barcelona also uses litigation to assert prerogatives. Turin has experimented with collaborative governance (beni comuni regulation). Athens lacks equivalent institutional venues and relies on informal party networks and clientelist ties
notes: Direct source for MCC 'intergovernmental coordination' sub-dimension

definition_evidence: Spain: conditional recourse to the Tribunal Constitucional plus ordinary courts. Italy: administrative courts (TAR) with regions escalating to the Corte Costituzionale. Greece: administrative supervision shifted from ex ante approval to ex post legality checks, but Athens lacks direct constitutional remedies and depends on the Council of State for narrow legality review only
notes: Direct source for the MCC 'conflict-resolution capacity' sub-dimension -- confirms Greece has the narrowest judicial avenue of the three

construct: Civil society mobilisation as institutionalisation differentiator
definition_evidence: Turin institutionalised citizen involvement via the Regolamento dei Beni Comuni (legal force for co-governance). Barcelona blends grassroots movements (PAH) with institutionalised platforms (Decidim). Athens shows some of Europe's most dynamic grassroots responses (solidarity networks refugee squats mutual aid) but without formal channels, risking fragmented/precarious welfare provision and depoliticisation of structural inequalities
notes: Feeds the 'Participation' and 'Institutionalisation' sub-dimensions of MRCI (spec Sec.5.3)

definition_evidence: A 2024 survey across 12 prefectures found only 98 of 510 integration classes for migrant/refugee children were adequately prepared, citing teacher shortages and lack of training
notes: Direct quantitative data point for education coverage/accessibility indicators

definition_evidence: Only about 15% of children with disabilities in Greece attend school due to inaccessible infrastructure lack of adapted services and insufficient resources despite a strong legal framework (Law 3699/2008)
notes: Illustrates the thesis's recurring pattern: strong legal text + weak implementation. Relevant to the Inclusion Gap indicator (spec Sec.5.5)

definition_evidence: Launched 2016, reached over 55 schools involving 1000 teachers and 5000 students
Only 29% of Roma children complete primary education and just 2% finish secondary school in metropolitan Athens
notes: One of the starkest Inclusion Gap figures found in the thesis -- strong candidate for the Inclusion Gap indicator (spec Sec.5.5)

construct: Private tutoring dependence / social tutoring response
definition_evidence: By 2014 nearly all final-year secondary students in Athens received private tutoring (frontistirio) outside school; in response a 2013 study found 31 social-tutoring initiatives in Greater Athens (20 municipal), and the Athens municipal Social Tutoring Centre (est. 2012) had supported ~1200 students by 2018
notes: Illustrates municipal compensation for a systemic accessibility failure (undermines free public education in principle)

definition_evidence: Turin's role in health coverage is facilitative rather than substantive: it helps residents navigate the national system (SSN) via offices like InformaStranieri e Nomadi and InforAnziani, while NGOs and faith-based associations (Sermig, GrIS Piemonte network) provide primary/mental-health care to undocumented migrants where legal coverage is absent
notes: ASSESSMENT section verbatim conclusion: 'Turin's contribution should be understood not as extensive in absolute terms, but as significant within the narrow scope of its competences'

construct: Health -- integrated planning with structural limits
definition_evidence: Barcelona advances health through integrated planning (superblocks, Green Corridors) and targeted programmes (dental, mental health, youth) but is structurally circumscribed: CatSalut retains primary clinical responsibility, and the padron (municipal registration) is a prerequisite for healthcare access -- meaning municipal registration policy directly determines health-access inclusion
notes: Recent restrictions on padron registration flagged by the thesis as a new obstacle to inclusion -- direct link to the Administrative Conditionality indicator (spec Sec.5.5)

definition_evidence: ERP (public housing) dwellings represent only 3.4% of Turin's total housing stock, with annual allocations far below demand; migrants are disproportionately represented among applicants but face indirect barriers
notes: Directly comparable to the Barcelona and Athens public-housing-stock figures -- core City x Right x Year data point

definition_evidence: Public housing accounts for less than 2% of Barcelona's residential stock far below the European average while demand vastly outstrips supply
notes: Confirms Barcelona has an even smaller public stock share than Turin despite stronger regulatory tools -- important nuance for any composite score (capacity/commitment does not equal stock coverage)

definition_evidence: Barcelona households devote on average 46% of income to rent; rents rose approximately 70% over the last decade, about four times faster than salaries; evictions continue in the thousands each year
value_type: quantitative (46% income-to-rent; +70% rent decade-on-decade vs wages)
notes: Strong quantitative accessibility/affordability figures -- direct input for the impact.csv 'accessibility' field and for outcome_variables

definition_evidence: Barcelona's tanteig i retracte (right of first refusal), 30% inclusionary zoning requirement, and 2028 ban on new short-term rental licences illustrate creative extension of municipal competences -- but subject to judicial curtailment (STS 37/2022 struck down a proposed surcharge on vacant dwellings)
notes: documentary + case law
column12: Good evidence for both the MRCI 'innovation' sub-dimension and the Vertical Friction Index (spec Sec.6) via the STS 37/2022 litigation example

construct: Education -- territorial inequality and demographic decline
definition_evidence: Central Turin districts have a dense network of services while peripheral areas (higher concentration of foreign/low-income families) show lower enrolment rates and more fragile infrastructure; demographic decline (shrinking school-age population) has caused school closures in some areas while demand remains unmet in others, requiring difficult efficiency/equity trade-offs
notes: Closing synthesis paragraph for Turin-Education (no ASSESSMENT header, but structurally equivalent). Directly supports the Territorial Equity indicator (spec Sec.5.5)

definition_evidence: 'In a Commitment-Impact Matrix, Turin would rank high in commitment but only moderate-to-high in impact, reflecting the tension between ambition and constraint' -- attributed causes: national fiscal rules, demographic trends, structural inequalities outside municipal control
notes: Confirms and completes the citation already in the codebook (previously captured from a partial view) -- this is the thesis's single explicit application of its own commitment-impact matrix

construct: Education -- expanded competences via Consorci d'Educacio
definition_evidence: Barcelona's scope extends beyond basic municipal duties (school planning, admissions, vocational training, adult education, cultural learning) via the hybrid Consorci d'Educacio de Barcelona. Flagship commitments: City Agreement for Education 2030, expansion of Escoles Bressol (early childhood), institutionalised participation via Consell d'Educacio Municipal and Consell d'Innovacio Pedagogica, and Barcelona Activa linking adult education/vocational training to employment
notes: documentary
column13: same structural role as the other 6 ASSESSMENT blocks) -- strongest MRCI institutionalisation example found in the education chapter

construct: Education -- territorial disparities despite broad competences
definition_evidence: Districts with high migrant/low-income populations face limited public provision and greater reliance on concertados (subsidised private schools), reinforcing ethnic and socio-economic segregation; housing insecurity further destabilises educational continuity
notes: Explicitly echoes the Turin territorial-inequality finding (IMPACT_TUR_EDU_01) -- thesis notes this parallel itself, useful for cross-city Territorial Equity comparison

construct: Health -- pragmatic adaptation with modest impact
definition_evidence: Athens' key strengths are pragmatic adaptation: municipal clinics, the 'I Care' programme, and KYADA social services extend primary care/social support to vulnerable groups; heatwave resilience measures link health with urban planning. Partnerships with solidarity clinics/NGOs were decisive for migrants, the homeless, and low-income residents especially during/after the financial crisis
notes: ASSESSMENT (lowercase heading) -- completes the set of six per-city-per-right synthesis blocks (all 9 combinations of 3 cities x 3 rights now captured except the chapter is 3 rights x 3 cities = 9 total; this is the 9th and final one)

definition_evidence: The absence of Athens-specific disaggregated health data hampers evaluation and targeted planning; municipal initiatives often rely on voluntary labour, EU-funded projects, or donations, making provision precarious, including closures/evictions of key solidarity clinics
notes: Direct evidence for the External Dependency Index (spec Sec.6) and for a 'data availability' flag in the domain data-availability matrix (spec Sec.8)
